lessons.current_goal: Use this lesson's language to count and report quantities or simple number relationships, using one, two, and fifteen.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to count and confirm small quantities in everyday adult tasks.
lessons.current_can_do: I can report quantities and understand simple number information, using relevant words such as one, eight, and fifteen.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can understand and use numbers from one to fifteen to count familiar people and objects.
lessons.current_reading_text: Mariam is preparing a meeting room for fifteen people. She puts one projector at the front and two extension leads near the wall. Three water jugs and four tables are ready before she brings in five signs and six spare chairs. She counts seven folders, eight pens, nine name cards, ten cups, eleven notepads, twelve badges, thirteen forms, and fourteen handouts. When she sees all fifteen seats in place, she knows the room is ready.
lessons.updated_reading_text: Maya is preparing a small meeting room before colleagues arrive. She counts six chairs, eight water bottles, and ten printed agendas, then checks whether the numbers match the booking. A coworker brings three more cups and one spare notebook. Together they recount the supplies and confirm that the room is ready without using complicated calculations.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Build confidence using sixteen, seventeen, and million to count and report quantities or simple number relationships in a short adult-life context.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to understand and state larger numbers used in prices, rooms, queues, and totals.
lessons.current_can_do: I can use sixteen, fifty, and million when I report quantities and understand simple number information.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can recognize and say common numbers from sixteen to one million in familiar practical contexts.
lessons.current_reading_text: A hotel worker checks a booking screen before a busy weekend. Room requests include sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, and twenty guests. Larger group bookings show thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, and ninety people. The conference summary shows one hundred places. One report records one thousand bookings, while the company website records one million visits across all its locations.

lessons.current_goal: Recognize and use first, second, and equals while learning to count and report quantities or simple number relationships.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to use ordinal numbers and basic calculation words in simple practical tasks.
lessons.current_can_do: I can understand and use first, eighth, and division to report quantities and understand simple number information.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can understand basic position words and simple arithmetic language in familiar situations.
lessons.current_reading_title: A Queue and a Training Exercise
lessons.current_reading_text: At a service centre, customers are called in order. The first person goes to Desk A, the second to Desk B, and the third waits near the door. The fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth customers follow as desks become free. Later, staff practise simple addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. The trainer writes a short calculation and asks whether the result equals the total on the screen.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A training coordinator checks a short score sheet after a workshop. One team is first, another is second, and a third team is third. The coordinator also reviews a simple total using addition and subtraction, then checks whether the final figures equal the expected result. Multiplication and division appear only in a few basic examples on the sheet.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Practise using this lesson's language to count and report quantities or simple number relationships, including plus, minus, and percentage.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to understand common calculation symbols and percentage language in everyday transactions.
lessons.current_can_do: I can complete a short real-life task where I need to report quantities and understand simple number information, including language such as plus, times, and percentage.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can follow very simple calculations using plus, minus, times, divided by, and percentage.
lessons.current_reading_text: Nadia checks an invoice before sending it to a client. She uses plus to add a delivery fee and minus to remove a discount. One line shows three items times the unit price. Another cost is divided by two because two departments share it. At the bottom, a percentage is used for tax. Nadia checks every line before she approves the total.
lessons.updated_reading_text: At a café, Karim checks the bill before paying. The cashier explains that one item is added with plus, a discount is shown with minus, and a percentage applies to the final amount. Karim asks how the total was calculated. The cashier shows the simple steps, including times and divided by, so he can confirm the amount.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Use this lesson's language to identify and describe colours in everyday choices, using red, blue, and indigo.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to identify and name common colours in clothing, signs, products, and everyday objects.
lessons.current_can_do: I can describe and compare colours in everyday choices, using relevant words such as red, brown, and indigo.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can understand and use common colour words to describe familiar objects.
lessons.current_reading_text: A designer prepares a simple colour palette for a café. The client compares red, blue, yellow, green, orange, purple, pink, brown, black, and white. For accent colours, the designer also tests cyan, magenta, lime, teal, and indigo before presenting the final options.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A shop manager and a designer are preparing a window display. They compare red, blue, yellow, green, black, and white items, then add orange and pink details for contrast. The manager wants the colours to be easy to distinguish from a distance. They agree on a simple palette that customers can recognize quickly.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Build confidence using violet, coral, and neutral to identify and describe colours in everyday choices in a short adult-life context.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to describe colour shades and visual intensity in practical design and shopping contexts.
lessons.current_can_do: I can use violet, bright, and neutral when I describe and compare colours in everyday choices.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can use simple colour modifiers such as light, dark, bright, pale, warm, and cool.
lessons.current_reading_text: An interior designer compares violet, coral, salmon, turquoise, and lavender samples. Under different light, some colours look light or dark, bright or dull, vivid or pale. The designer also compares deep shades with warm, cool, and neutral choices before recommending a balanced room palette.
lessons.updated_reading_text: At a paint counter, an adult customer compares several colour samples for a home office. One green is light, another is dark, and a blue sample looks pale beside a vivid turquoise. The assistant explains which colours feel warm, cool, or neutral in the room. The customer chooses a bright but calm shade for the main wall.

lessons.current_can_do: I can understand and use mix, saturation, and pigment to describe and compare colours in everyday choices.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can understand simple language about mixing colours, shades, tints, and colour changes.
lessons.current_reading_text: Before a poster goes to print, a designer may mix and blend colours, adjust a shade or tint, and compare the hue. The team checks saturation and smooths a gradient. A rainbow is useful for discussing the spectrum, while pigment affects the colour in physical paint.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A junior designer prepares a colour sample for a poster. She mixes two pigments, then blends them until the hue looks even. Next, she adjusts the tint and saturation and checks the gradient on screen. Before sending the file, she compares the final colours with a printed spectrum to make sure the result is consistent.

lessons.current_goal: Practise using this lesson's language to identify shapes and basic geometric features in practical objects, including circle, square, and pyramid.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to identify common two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes in everyday objects.

lessons.updated_can_do: Can name familiar shapes and match them to common objects and designs.
lessons.current_reading_text: A packaging designer reviews simple and three-dimensional forms for a new product box. The first sketch includes a circle, a square, a triangle, a rectangle, and an oval. Another drawing shows a diamond, a pentagon, a hexagon, an octagon, and a star. The review also covers a sphere, a cube, a cylinder, a cone, and a pyramid.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A packaging designer reviews several simple product containers. A label uses a circle and a square, while the front panel includes a triangle and rectangle. Nearby samples show a cube, cylinder, cone, and pyramid. The designer checks each shape carefully so the cutting template and product layout are easy for the production team to follow.

lessons.updated_goal: Learn to identify common lines, angles, and less familiar solid shapes in simple diagrams.
lessons.current_can_do: I can identify and describe shapes, lines and basic geometry, using relevant words such as prism, straight, and perpendicular.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can recognize basic line and angle terms and distinguish simple geometric forms.
lessons.current_reading_text: A technician checks a drawing before parts are produced. The first sketch includes prism, cuboid, hemisphere, torus, and tetrahedron. Another drawing shows line, curve, straight, zigzag, and spiral. The review also covers right angle, acute angle, obtuse angle, parallel, and perpendicular.
lessons.updated_reading_text: An apprentice looks at a simple technical sketch with a straight line, a curve, and a zigzag path. The trainer points out a right angle and shows how parallel lines stay apart while perpendicular lines meet at ninety degrees. A prism and a hemisphere appear in a separate diagram. The apprentice uses the labels to compare each feature.

lessons.current_goal: Build confidence using area, perimeter, and fractal to identify shapes and basic geometric features in practical objects in a short adult-life context.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to understand basic measurement and pattern vocabulary used in rooms, diagrams, and designs.
lessons.current_can_do: I can use area, symmetry, and fractal when I identify and describe shapes, lines and basic geometry.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can identify simple geometry terms such as area, perimeter, radius, pattern, and symmetry.
lessons.current_reading_text: An interior designer checks measurements and geometric relationships in a room plan. The first sketch includes area, perimeter, volume, radius, and diameter. Another drawing shows circumference, diagonal, symmetry, vertex, and edge. The review also covers repeat, sequence, pattern, tessellation, and fractal.
lessons.updated_reading_text: An interior designer checks a room plan before ordering materials. She measures the area and perimeter, then reviews the radius and diameter of a round table. A diagonal line helps position the furniture, while symmetry keeps the layout balanced. She also checks a repeating floor pattern so the tiles continue neatly across the room.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Recognize and use grid, array, and kaleidoscope while learning to identify shapes and basic geometric features in practical objects.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to recognize grid-based layouts and repeated visual arrangements in everyday design.
lessons.current_can_do: I can understand and use grid, matrix, and kaleidoscope to identify and describe shapes, lines and basic geometry.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can identify a grid, array, matrix, mosaic, and kaleidoscope in simple visual contexts.
lessons.current_reading_text: A graphic designer builds a repeating visual for a wall panel. The first sketch includes grid, array, matrix, mosaic, and kaleidoscope.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A graphic designer arranges small icons in a grid for a wall display. The icons form a regular array, and the working file stores their positions in a simple matrix. Another section uses a mosaic made from repeated shapes. For inspiration, the designer also studies a kaleidoscope pattern with strong symmetry and repetition.

lessons.current_goal: Practise using this lesson's language to say how someone feels and understand simple reasons, including happy, joyful, and frustrated.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to describe common positive and negative emotions in familiar adult situations.
lessons.current_can_do: I can complete a short real-life task where I need to describe how someone feels in a familiar situation, including language such as happy, delighted, and frustrated.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can use basic feeling words to say how someone feels after simple events.
lessons.current_reading_text: After a project presentation, different people react in different ways. One colleague feels happy and joyful, while another is excited and proud. A manager is grateful for the team's work and content with the result. During the celebration, people may feel amused, delighted, cheerful, or hopeful. If plans change suddenly, someone may instead feel sad, angry, scared, worried, or frustrated.
lessons.updated_reading_text: After a team presentation, several colleagues react differently. Lina feels happy and proud because the client liked the work, while Samir is grateful for the team's support. Another colleague is excited about the next project. When a last-minute change appears, one person becomes worried and another feels frustrated, but the group stays hopeful.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Use this lesson's language to say how someone feels and understand simple reasons, using disappointed, upset, and alert.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to describe everyday emotional states during work, travel, and social situations.
lessons.current_can_do: I can describe how someone feels in a familiar situation, using relevant words such as disappointed, surprised, and alert.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can recognize and use common words for feelings such as tired, calm, confused, and surprised.
lessons.current_reading_text: A long workday can bring many reactions. A person may feel disappointed or upset after bad news, annoyed by a delay, bored during a long wait, or lonely when working alone. A quiet break can help someone feel calm or relaxed. Later they may be tired or sleepy, surprised by a message, confused by instructions, curious about a change, thoughtful about a decision, indifferent to a minor issue, or alert after some rest.
lessons.updated_reading_text: After a long shift, Hala feels tired and a little bored while waiting for transport. A delayed message leaves her confused, then a colleague calls with surprising news. During the ride home, she becomes calmer and more relaxed. By the time she arrives, she is still sleepy but alert enough to prepare for the next morning.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Build confidence using hungry, thirsty, and comfortable to say how someone feels and understand simple reasons in a short adult-life context.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to describe common physical feelings and comfort states in everyday life.
lessons.current_can_do: I can use hungry, dizzy, and comfortable when I describe how someone feels in a familiar situation.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can say when someone feels hungry, thirsty, hot, cold, tired, or comfortable.
lessons.current_reading_text: During a busy day, people notice physical states as well as emotions. Someone may be hungry, thirsty, or full after a meal. A hot room can make one person feel hot while another feels cold. If someone feels dizzy or nauseous, they may stop and rest. After a demanding shift, a person can feel exhausted; after good rest, they may feel energetic and comfortable.
lessons.updated_reading_text: During a busy afternoon, Omar tells a coworker that he feels hungry and thirsty. The room is hot, and after standing for a long time he becomes slightly dizzy, so he sits down and drinks water. Later he feels less tired and more comfortable. His coworker checks that he is okay before they return to work.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Recognize and use mother, father, and oldest child while learning to talk about family relationships, routines and support.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to identify close family members and describe basic family relationships.
lessons.current_can_do: I can understand and use mother, siblings, and oldest Child to identify family relationships and talk about shared activities.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can name close family members and understand simple statements about family relationships.
lessons.current_reading_text: At a family dinner, Salma sits with her mother and father. Her sister arrives with a baby, and her brother brings his son and daughter. The parents are happy to see all the siblings together. One cousin is a twin. During the meal, the family uses everyday words such as mom and dad. Salma's big sister helps the little brother with his plate, while the oldest child tells everyone about school.
lessons.updated_reading_text: Nadia shows a new colleague a family photo on her phone. She points to her mother and father, then introduces her sister and brother. She also explains which people are her parents and siblings and mentions that one relative has a baby. The conversation stays simple and friendly, helping the colleague understand who each person is.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Practise using this lesson's language to talk about family relationships, routines and support, including youngest child, middle child, and homework help.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to talk about family roles, shared routines, and common activities.
lessons.current_can_do: I can complete a short real-life task where I need to identify family relationships and talk about shared activities, including language such as youngest Child, road Trip, and homework Help.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can understand simple descriptions of family roles and everyday activities done together.
lessons.current_reading_text: A family group is planning a weekend together. The youngest child wants game night, the middle child suggests a movie night, and the only child in another household joins the holiday gathering. A stepmother and stepfather help organise a family dinner, road trip, cooking together, a bedtime story, a morning routine, a family photo, and homework help.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A family is planning a weekend together. The youngest child wants game night, while the middle child suggests a movie night and the only child from another household joins the visit. Their stepmother and stepfather help organize a family dinner and a short road trip. Everyone also plans a family photo before the weekend ends.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Use this lesson's language to talk about family relationships, routines and support, using love, trust, and heritage.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to talk about support, care, trust, and other qualities in family relationships.
lessons.current_can_do: I can identify family relationships and talk about shared activities, using relevant words such as love, guidance, and heritage.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can understand and use simple words for positive family support and relationships.
lessons.current_reading_text: Healthy family relationships can include love, trust, support, and care. Adults may also provide protection and guidance, while discipline should be fair and respectful. Affection can strengthen a bond, and family heritage can connect people with earlier generations.
lessons.updated_reading_text: Strong family relationships often grow through love, trust, support, and care. Adults may offer protection and guidance when someone faces a difficult decision. Affection can strengthen a bond, while fair discipline helps set clear limits. Families may also share stories, traditions, and heritage that connect younger and older generations. over time.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Build confidence using bed, nightstand, and duvet to name bedroom items and describe where they are or how they are used in a short adult-life context.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to name common bedroom furniture and bedding and describe where items are placed.
lessons.current_can_do: I can use bed, mirror, and duvet when I name bedroom items and say where they are.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can identify common bedroom furniture and bedding and say where basic items are.
lessons.current_reading_text: An adult is preparing a bedroom for everyday use. Before unpacking, the tenant checks bed, nightstand, dresser, wardrobe, and desk. Next, the room is arranged with chair, bookshelf, mirror, stool, and chest of drawers. The final check covers pillow, blanket, sheet, mattress, and duvet. Anything damaged or missing is added to a short maintenance list.
lessons.updated_reading_text: A tenant checks the bedroom before unpacking. The bed is beside a nightstand, while a dresser and wardrobe provide storage for clothes. A desk, chair, bookshelf, mirror, and stool complete the work and dressing area. The tenant also checks the pillow, blanket, sheet, mattress, and duvet before reporting any damaged or missing item.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Recognize and use pillowcase, comforter, and outlet while learning to name bedroom items and describe where they are or how they are used.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to name bedroom fittings, soft furnishings, and basic electrical features.
lessons.current_can_do: I can understand and use pillowcase, window, and outlet to name bedroom items and say where they are.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can identify common bedroom fittings and say how simple items such as lamps, curtains, and outlets are used.
lessons.current_reading_text: An adult is preparing a bedroom for everyday use. Before unpacking, the tenant checks pillowcase, comforter, cushion, bed frame, and headboard. Next, the room is arranged with lamp, curtain, window, door, and rug. The final check covers carpet, ceiling light, light switch, blinds, and outlet. Anything damaged or missing is added to a short maintenance list.
lessons.updated_reading_text: Before a guest arrives, Sara checks the bedding and room fittings. She puts a clean pillowcase on the pillow, straightens the comforter, and moves a cushion onto the chair. She checks the bed frame, headboard, lamp, curtains, blinds, and window. Finally, she tests the ceiling light, light switch, and electrical outlet.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Practise using this lesson's language to name bedroom items and describe where they are or how they are used, including alarm clock, picture frame, and poster.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to name small bedroom objects, clothing items, and personal room accessories.
lessons.current_can_do: I can complete a short real-life task where I need to name bedroom items and say where they are, including language such as alarm Clock, tissue Box, and poster.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can identify common bedroom accessories and understand simple statements about where they belong.
lessons.current_reading_text: An adult is preparing a bedroom for everyday use. Before unpacking, the tenant checks alarm clock, picture frame, clock, plant, and vase. Next, the room is arranged with candle, calendar, tissue box, wastebasket, and hanger. The final check covers pajamas, slippers, robe, teddy bear, and poster. Anything damaged or missing is added to a short maintenance list.
lessons.updated_reading_text: Before sleeping, Yusuf tidies the room for the next morning. He sets the alarm clock, straightens a picture frame, and checks the calendar beside the desk. A tissue box and wastebasket stay within easy reach, while clothes go on a hanger. He places his pajamas, slippers, and robe neatly away and leaves the room ready for the night.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.

lessons.current_goal: Use this lesson's language to name bedroom items and describe where they are or how they are used, using books, photo album, and remote control.
lessons.updated_goal: Learn to name common personal and electronic items kept in a bedroom.
lessons.current_can_do: I can name bedroom items and say where they are, using relevant words such as books, charger, and remote Control.
lessons.updated_can_do: Can identify everyday personal devices and belongings and say where they are kept or used.
lessons.current_reading_text: An adult is preparing a bedroom for everyday use. Before unpacking, the tenant checks books, photo album, glasses, backpack, and jewelry box. Next, the room is arranged with phone, charger, laptop, headphones, and tablet. The final check covers speaker, reading light, and remote control. Anything damaged or missing is added to a short maintenance list.
lessons.updated_reading_text: Before bed, Mariam prepares the things she will need in the morning. She places her glasses beside a photo album and books, then packs a backpack and checks her phone. The charger, laptop, headphones, and tablet are ready on the desk. A speaker, reading light, and remote control remain nearby so the room stays organized.
lessons.editor_notes: Pre-A1 adult-learning objective, Can-Do statement, genre and 50–90 word reading reviewed for clarity, practical relevance and CEFR-appropriate support.
